title: Letting it go vs. never letting it go
core: Every word here sits downstream of an injury: someone was wronged, and someone has the standing to punish, protest, or strike back. The group splits on what happens to that entitlement — it is waived, deferred, formally erased, or kept forever. The second thing to track is *what kind of thing* each word names: a private feeling, a single act, a verdict, or a permanent standing condition. Sentence completions live in that second distinction more often than in the first.

words.nuance: The only word here that praises a **character**, and it is unearnable without power: you must have been the winner, the wronged party, the one holding the knife. **Magnanimous** is the grand gesture from above — the victor toasting the loser — where the others merely describe not acting.

**Forbear** is the quiet, ongoing *not-doing* of a specific blow you are entitled to deliver — the creditor who doesn't foreclose, the reviewer who forbore comment. The grievance is intact and the judgment unchanged; only the hand is stayed, and it can be unstayed tomorrow.

The one release word that is an accusation. **Condone** means the wrong was yours to protest and you looked away, so it implies complicity rather than mercy — which is why it almost always appears as *"I do not condone"*, drawing a line between the speaker and someone else.

**Relent** is the *moment of reversal*, and it requires a prior stretch of hardness to reverse: you were the one refusing, punishing, or pressing, and you finally softened. Alone in this group it also works on impersonal pressure — rain, heat, a fever relents.

Not mercy at all: **exonerate** doesn't waive the blame, it deletes it, on the finding that there was nothing to forgive. It is third-party and official — a court, an inquiry, a lab — never a feeling you have about your brother-in-law.

**Implacable** is defined by what fails against it: apology, concession, and plea all bounce off. That makes it the word for *forces* as much as people — the implacable tide, the implacable deadline — and applied to resolve rather than malice it can even read as admiration.

Where implacable resists persuasion, **obdurate** resists *pity* — the widow begs and you feel nothing. It is a verdict on the heart, not the will, and the speaker is condemning you, not merely reporting that you won't budge.

The only **act** in the hostile half, and a cool one: **retaliate** is a counter-move, not a state of mind — tariffs, sanctions, a strike back in kind. It needs a first blow to exist, so using it quietly assigns fault to the other side, but it claims no moral high ground the way *avenge* does.

Purely internal and purely stored: **resent** is the grievance nursed in silence for months, always carrying the claim *"I deserved better."* Nothing is done and nothing is said — which is why it reflects badly on the holder, hostility with no discharge.

A noun naming a **relationship**, not a feeling or an act. **Enmity** can lie completely dormant — two houses at enmity for eighty years without a word — and it is typically mutual, often inherited, and reserved for clans, nations, and factions rather than irritating coworkers.

exam_note: The traps are the near-misses, not the opposites: **condone** ≠ forgive (it's tolerating a wrong you still call wrong), **exonerate** ≠ pardon (pardon presumes guilt, exoneration denies it), and **obdurate** vs. **implacable** turns on whether it's pity or persuasion that fails.
